strengths: Principled theoretical formulation: The paper elegantly integrates learnable order dynamics into variable-length discrete flow matching via continuous-time Markov chains and projected rate matching.

Tractable and simulation-free training: By parameterizing insertion and unmasking event times with Kumaraswamy distributions sharing a common shape parameter, the authors obtain closed-form marginals and likelihoods, enabling joint training of the generator and target rate networks without expensive trajectory simulation.

Efficient gradient estimation: The two-sample leave-one-out score function gradient estimator with stop-gradient allows updating both target and generator networks within a single autograd backward pass.

Insightful analysis and verification: On the star graph traversal benchmark, the authors convincingly demonstrate that the model learns the known locally optimal order (endpoints inward to the junction), yielding dramatic gains on the hard split (Exact Match jumping from ~7.4% to ~88.1%).

Consistent generation gains: On de novo molecule generation (SAFE dataset), LFlexMDM achieves noticeable improvements in sample validity and quality over the standard uniform-schedule FlexMDM baseline across multiple inference step budgets.
weaknesses: Limited experimental breadth: Evaluation is confined to synthetic graph traversal and small molecule generation on the SAFE dataset. Benchmarking on broader sequence modeling domains, such as natural language or protein sequence modeling, would have significantly broadened the impact.

Sensitivity and stability constraints during optimization: Training the unmasking rate parameter directly proved unstable and required fixing bum=1 in practice, along with custom schedule regularization penalties (Appendix D.5.2) to prevent endpoint probability collapse.

Missing comparisons with contemporaneous edit models: While the paper thoroughly compares against FlexMDM, empirical comparisons against other recent insertion/edit flow approaches (such as EditFlows or ILM) under identical compute settings are missing.
Minor presentation issues: A few typos and repetition are present in the text (e.g., 'simultaneous simultaneous' on page 8, and citations of 2026/forthcoming preprints).

strengths: Sound and elegant theoretical formulation: The paper nicely generalizes projected Discrete Flow Matching (DFM) to incorporate data-dependent, learnable arrival and unmasking rates without requiring full trajectory simulations.

Clever choice of parameterization: Employing a truncated Kumaraswamy distribution with shared shape parameter a enables exact closed-form expressions for both hazard rates and the intermediate state likelihoods, avoiding expensive numerical integration during training.

Efficient training algorithm: Combining a 2-sample REINFORCE leave-one-out baseline with pathwise loss gradients allows joint optimization of the target order dynamics (phi) and the generator (theta) in a single autograd backward pass.

Convincing proof of concept on algorithmic graphs: On the star graph traversal benchmark, the model demonstrates the ability to discover the locally optimal generation order (moving from outer leaves toward the junction), leading to dramatic performance improvements on the hard setting (up to ~88% exact match vs ~7% for FlexMDM).

Comprehensive empirical analysis on molecular generation: The method achieves notable improvements in sample validity and quality over the FlexMDM baseline across multiple sampling budgets and auxiliary network sizes.
weaknesses: Training stability constraints: Joint optimization of both insertion (b_in) and unmasking (b_um) hazard rates is prone to severe training instability and schedule degeneracy (Figures 6 and 9), forcing the authors to freeze b_um = 1 and rely on ad-hoc schedule regularization penalties (Appendix D.5.2).

Computational overhead and performance gap of the shared architecture: The best-performing setup requires a separate auxiliary transformer network. When using a shared backbone, performance drops substantially on challenging tasks (e.g., on hard star graph traversal without confidence selection, 34.2% vs 87.9%).

Limited evaluation domains: The empirical evaluation is restricted to synthetic star graphs and small molecule sequence generation (SAFE dataset). Key variable-length discrete domains such as natural language generation or protein sequences are not explored.

Diversity-quality trade-offs: The reported improvements in validity and quality in Table 2 and Table 7 correlate with noticeable reductions in diversity and uniqueness (especially under greedy or low-temperature nucleus sampling), raising questions about potential sample diversity degradation.

strengths: Principled and elegant mathematical formulation: The paper successfully extends Discrete Flow Matching (DFM) and projected CTMCs to incorporate data-dependent, learnable order dynamics for variable-length sequence generation.

Efficient training without trajectory simulation: By parameterizing the event schedules via the Kumaraswamy distribution with shared power parameter $a$, the marginal likelihood $p_t^\phi(z|z_1)$ is obtained in closed form. This enables training the generator and the auxiliary schedule network simultaneously via a low-variance leave-one-out REINFORCE estimator in a single backward pass, completely bypassing costly full-trajectory rollouts.

Insightful analysis of generation dynamics: The star graph traversal experiments provide clear empirical verification that LFlexMDM learns the optimal generation order (from arm endpoints inward to the junction), backed by quantitative correlation analysis (Figure 5) and sample traces.

Strong empirical results over standard baselines: On de novo molecule generation (SAFE dataset), LFlexMDM substantially improves chemical validity (up to 99.9%) and molecule quality (up to 62.1% vs 39.5% for vanilla FlexMDM) across various inference budgets and sampling configurations.

Thorough and transparent appendix: The supplementary material provides complete proofs for all propositions (KFE satisfaction, projected rate matching KL bounds, Kumaraswamy ordering probabilities), detailed pseudo-code, and explicit ablation studies.
weaknesses: Limited evaluation domains: The method is tested only on synthetic star graph traversal and small molecule generation. Given that variable-length sequence generation and insertion models are frequently motivated by natural language processing and protein modeling, demonstrating results on standard language generation benchmarks would significantly broaden the paper's impact.

Theoretical understanding of stability trade-offs: The finding that making the unmasking rate $b_{um}$ learnable destabilizes training—necessitating fixing $b_{um}=1$—is observed empirically, but lacks an in-depth theoretical analysis explaining why co-adapting both insertion and unmasking rates leads to numerical degeneracy or high gradient variance.

Computational overhead quantification: While the gradient estimator is shown to require only a single autograd pass with two samples, the paper does not report empirical wall-clock training times, memory overhead, or throughput comparisons between LFlexMDM and vanilla FlexMDM.

Minor presentation issues and typos: There are a few minor typographic inconsistencies, such as 'LNFlexMDM' instead of 'LFlexMDM' in Table 4/5 headers, 'exiting works' instead of 'existing works' on page 5, and 'implemenetation' on page 8.
